questions.question: An EF Core endpoint works correctly with 10,000 rows but becomes extremely slow after the table grows to 50 million rows. The code calls ToList() before filtering. What would you change and how would you prove it?
questions.shortAnswer: I would first inspect the generated SQL and execution plan rather than assuming the ORM is the problem. If ToList materializes the full table before filtering, the application is moving far more data than necessary. I would keep the query as IQueryable, apply filters, projection and pagination before materialization, then inspect the SQL and database plan. I would also verify supporting indexes and measure rows read, duration and network payload.
questions.detailedAnswer: I would first inspect the generated SQL and execution plan rather than assuming the ORM is the problem. If ToList materializes the full table before filtering, the application is moving far more data than necessary. I would keep the query as IQueryable, apply filters, projection and pagination before materialization, then inspect the SQL and database plan. I would also verify supporting indexes and measure rows read, duration and network payload. The key is controlling where computation happens. IQueryable lets the provider translate the expression to SQL, but I still validate the generated SQL because not every expression translates efficiently. I would avoid returning IQueryable across broad architectural boundaries unless its lifetime and ownership are well understood.
questions.example: Instead of loading all orders and then calling Where in memory, I would build the EF query with Where, Select and Take/Skip and materialize only the required rows.
questions.seniorPerspective: The key is controlling where computation happens. questions.question: An ASP.NET Core API is timing out under load. You find several .Result and .Wait() calls around HTTP and database operations. Walk me through how you would investigate and fix it.
questions.shortAnswer: I would not start by simply converting everything to async. First I would confirm whether the latency is caused by blocked ThreadPool threads, downstream latency, connection-pool pressure, or something else. I would look at request latency, ThreadPool counters, traces and dependency timings. If synchronous waits are blocking request threads while I/O is pending, I would make the call chain asynchronous end to end, pass CancellationToken through it, and remove blocking waits. Then I would load-test the same traffic pattern and compare p95/p99 latency and ThreadPool behavior before and after the change.
questions.detailedAnswer: I would not start by simply converting everything to async. First I would confirm whether the latency is caused by blocked ThreadPool threads, downstream latency, connection-pool pressure, or something else. I would look at request latency, ThreadPool counters, traces and dependency timings. If synchronous waits are blocking request threads while I/O is pending, I would make the call chain asynchronous end to end, pass CancellationToken through it, and remove blocking waits. Then I would load-test the same traffic pattern and compare p95/p99 latency and ThreadPool behavior before and after the change. I would distinguish scalability from raw execution speed: async does not make the database query faster. It prevents a request thread from being occupied unnecessarily. I would also check for hidden synchronous calls in libraries, unbounded fan-out, connection limits and cancellation behavior.
questions.example: For example, an API calls a database and a downstream REST service. If each request blocks a worker thread while waiting for I/O, concurrency can exhaust available threads. With await on both operations, the thread is returned while the I/O is pending and can serve other requests.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would distinguish scalability from raw execution speed: async does not make the database query faster. It prevents a request thread from being occupied unnecessarily. I would also check for hidden synchronous calls in libraries, unbounded fan-out, connection limits and cancellation behavior.
questions.commonMistakes: I would watch ThreadPool queue length, request p95/p99, dependency latency, active requests, DB connection pool usage and timeout/cancellation rates. A successful fix should improve concurrency without simply moving the bottleneck to the database.
followUps: How would you prove ThreadPool starvation rather than assume it?
What happens if one of the parallel calls fails?
Would you use Task.WhenAll for every downstream call?

questions.question: An endpoint needs data from four independent downstream services and currently calls them one after another. Latency is too high. How would you redesign the flow without overwhelming the dependencies?
questions.shortAnswer: I would first confirm that the four calls are genuinely independent. If they are, I would start them concurrently and await Task.WhenAll, because the total latency can move closer to the slowest dependency instead of the sum of all four. I would still put limits around fan-out, propagate cancellation and define what happens when one dependency fails. I would measure the improvement and check downstream load because reducing our latency can increase pressure on another service.
questions.detailedAnswer: I would first confirm that the four calls are genuinely independent. If they are, I would start them concurrently and await Task.WhenAll, because the total latency can move closer to the slowest dependency instead of the sum of all four. I would still put limits around fan-out, propagate cancellation and define what happens when one dependency fails. I would measure the improvement and check downstream load because reducing our latency can increase pressure on another service. The senior decision is not 'parallel is always better'. I would check dependency rate limits, connection pools, failure semantics, response aggregation and whether partial results are acceptable. For large fan-out I would consider bounded concurrency rather than creating thousands of simultaneous tasks.
questions.example: If calls take roughly 150 ms, 200 ms, 300 ms and 250 ms sequentially, the endpoint may spend around 900 ms waiting. Running them concurrently can reduce waiting time toward the slowest call, subject to network and service overhead.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior decision is not 'parallel is always better'. I would check dependency rate limits, connection pools, failure semantics, response aggregation and whether partial results are acceptable. For large fan-out I would consider bounded concurrency rather than creating thousands of simultaneous tasks.

questions.question: A client disconnects while a long-running ASP.NET Core request is still querying a database and calling another service. How would you make the operation stop safely?
questions.shortAnswer: I would treat cancellation as part of the request contract. I would accept the request CancellationToken at the API boundary and pass it through service, HTTP and database calls wherever the underlying API supports it. I would avoid catching cancellation and turning it into a generic 500. I would also make sure cleanup still happens and that any background work that must outlive the request is deliberately separated from the request token.
questions.detailedAnswer: I would treat cancellation as part of the request contract. I would accept the request CancellationToken at the API boundary and pass it through service, HTTP and database calls wherever the underlying API supports it. I would avoid catching cancellation and turning it into a generic 500. I would also make sure cleanup still happens and that any background work that must outlive the request is deliberately separated from the request token. Cancellation is cooperative, not an instant kill. I would identify operations that can safely stop and make state changes idempotent if cancellation can happen between steps. For transactional work, I would decide whether cancellation should roll back or whether a durable workflow should continue independently.
questions.example: A report endpoint starts a database query and then calls a downstream service. If the browser closes the request, HttpContext.RequestAborted is signalled. Passing that token to EF Core and HttpClient lets those operations stop instead of continuing unnecessary work.
questions.seniorPerspective: Cancellation is cooperative, not an instant kill. I would identify operations that can safely stop and make state changes idempotent if cancellation can happen between steps. For transactional work, I would decide whether cancellation should roll back or whether a durable workflow should continue independently.
questions.commonMistakes: I would look for orphaned work, database commands that continue after request cancellation, swallowed OperationCanceledException and inconsistent partial state.

questions.question: You need an in-memory cache shared by many concurrent requests. A cache miss currently causes every request to call the database. How would you design it?
questions.shortAnswer: I would define the cache contract first: key scope, TTL, invalidation, maximum size and acceptable staleness. Then I would use a thread-safe data structure and prevent a cache stampede so concurrent misses do not all load the same value. I would also decide whether local memory is sufficient or whether the cache needs to be distributed across instances. Finally I would instrument hit rate, load latency and eviction behavior.
questions.detailedAnswer: I would define the cache contract first: key scope, TTL, invalidation, maximum size and acceptable staleness. Then I would use a thread-safe data structure and prevent a cache stampede so concurrent misses do not all load the same value. I would also decide whether local memory is sufficient or whether the cache needs to be distributed across instances. Finally I would instrument hit rate, load latency and eviction behavior. Concurrency correctness is only one part. A senior design also considers stale data, invalidation, memory pressure, multi-instance consistency, serialization cost and what happens when the cache is unavailable.
questions.example: If 200 requests arrive for the same product after expiry, I do not want 200 database queries. I would coordinate the first load and let the other callers await the same in-flight operation, with a bounded timeout.
questions.seniorPerspective: Concurrency correctness is only one part. A senior design also considers stale data, invalidation, memory pressure, multi-instance consistency, serialization cost and what happens when the cache is unavailable.
questions.commonMistakes: I would monitor hit ratio, miss bursts, cache size, eviction rate, database load and lock/contention time.

questions.question: An authenticated user changes a resource ID in the request and accesses another user's data. How would you identify the missing authorization check and enforce it server-side?
questions.shortAnswer: I would frame security as a trust-boundary problem. I would identify what is untrusted, where authorization is enforced, what data is sensitive and which operations have side effects. Then I would validate inputs, enforce authorization server-side, protect secrets, use least privilege and make security failures observable. I would not rely on a client-side check or a prompt as the security boundary.

The senior discussion is about defense in depth and failure modes: authentication proves identity, authorization decides access, and downstream systems must not assume an upstream check is sufficient.
